headline: Scientists may have found dinosaur blood cells in a bone

sources.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur's bone, say scientists (The Guardian)
Evidence of red blood cells seen in dinosaur fossil from Brazil (Reuters, via KFGO)
Incredible discovery of fossilized blood cells inside a dinosaur leg bone (New Atlas)

chunks.text: Scientists say they may have found [[red blood cells]] in the leg bone of a dinosaur that lived about 115 million years ago. The young [[meat-eating]] dinosaur's bone was {{dug up}} in a [[mine]] in northeastern Brazil in 2008. An international team {{laid out}} its [[evidence]] on November 2, 2026, in a [[science journal]]. When the team {{zoomed in}} with a powerful microscope, tiny round shapes {{showed up}} in [[narrow channels]] where [[blood vessels]] once ran.

chunks.text: Soft parts of the body usually {{break down}} fast, so they are [[rarely]] found in [[fossils]], the remains of ancient life kept in rock. The team says these shapes are now made of [[minerals]], hard natural materials. Chemical tests {{came back}} [[positive]] for heme, the part of blood that holds [[iron]] and helps carry oxygen. The team says those results {{back up}} its blood cell idea. The team also says one mineral may have helped {{hold the shapes together}}.

verbs.correct: To rot until nothing is left
verbs.wrong: To move deeper into the ground
verbs.why: Fallen leaves break down in the soil over the winter. Food scraps break down fast in warm, wet places. Soft parts of the body usually break down fast, so they are rarely found in fossils.

verbs.wrong: To be sent to a different lab
verbs.why: Most lab tests come back within a week. My test results usually come back on Friday. Chemical tests on the bone came back positive for heme.

verbs.correct: To support an idea with evidence
verbs.wrong: To print an idea in a journal

verbs.correct: To keep something in one piece

chunks.text: The study has {{stirred up}} [[debate]]. A leading dinosaur expert at North Carolina State University, in the U.S., is [[not convinced]]. She says dinosaur blood cells should be thicker in the middle. These shapes [[curve inward]], so she says they could {{turn out}} to be something else. She finds the chemical signs more convincing. The team cannot completely {{rule out}} microbes, tiny living things, as a source of the heme.

verbs.wrong: To test an idea a second time
verbs.why: New rules often stir up arguments at school. Political posts stir up arguments online. The study has stirred up debate among scientists.

verbs.correct: To be found to be something later
verbs.wrong: To stay hidden for a very long time
verbs.why: Many strange noises turn out to be the wind. Some rumors turn out to be false. An American expert says the round shapes could turn out to be something else.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To show that something is very common
verbs.why: Doctors rule out serious problems with a few simple tests. Police rule out theft when nothing is missing. The team says it cannot completely rule out microbes as a source of the heme.

chunks.text: The lead scientist, at a university in Australia, {{points out}} that the team did not find dinosaur DNA. "We have not found a [[vial]] of dinosaur blood," she said. This is not the [[plot]] of Jurassic Park, the movie where scientists {{bring dinosaurs back}} with old DNA. If the finding is [[confirmed]], researchers could {{figure out}} more about how active dinosaurs were. The lead scientist says more chemical [[clues]] may be waiting in museum fossils.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact

verbs.why: My doctor points out that sleep matters. Teachers point out that practice helps. The lead scientist points out that the team did not find dinosaur DNA.

verbs.wrong: To study an old bone very closely
verbs.why: Some scientists want to bring back the woolly mammoth, an extinct animal that no longer lives anywhere. No lab can bring back an extinct animal without its DNA. In the movie Jurassic Park, scientists bring dinosaurs back with old DNA.

verbs.correct: To learn something by studying it
verbs.why: Mechanics figure out what is wrong with a car. Students figure out the answer by testing their ideas. If the finding is confirmed, researchers could figure out how active dinosaurs were.

mainIdea.s: Researchers report what may be blood cells and chemical signs of blood in an ancient dinosaur bone from Brazil. Another expert has doubts about the shapes, and the team did not find any DNA.
mainIdea.why: Round shapes showed up in the bone and tests came back positive for heme. A U.S. expert says the shapes could turn out to be something else.

mainIdea.s: A team studying fossil material thinks small round forms in a very old leg bone may be dinosaur cells. One critic accepts their shape as correct, but she says the lab tests for heme were failures.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the critic doubts the shape of the cells. She finds the chemical signs more convincing, and the tests came back positive for heme.

mainIdea.s: Miners in South America have found a nearly complete skeleton of a giant plant eater. The national museum plans to show it to visitors next year after workers clean and repair each piece.
mainIdea.why: The news is about possible blood cells in one leg bone. It was dug up in 2008, and the team laid out its evidence in a science journal.

tf.s: The team found dinosaur DNA in the bone.
tf.why: The lead scientist points out that the team did not find dinosaur DNA.

tf.s: Tiny round shapes showed up inside a dinosaur's leg bone.
tf.why: The team saw the shapes with a powerful microscope, in channels where blood vessels once ran.

tf.s: A U.S. dinosaur expert is sure the shapes are real blood cells.
tf.why: She is not convinced. She says the shapes curve inward, so they could turn out to be something else.

tf.s: Chemical tests came back positive for heme, a part of blood.
tf.why: Heme holds iron and helps carry oxygen. The team says these results back up its idea.

tf.s: The team has ruled out microbes as a source of the heme.
tf.why: The team says it cannot completely rule out microbes, so the source of the heme is still open to question.

tf.s: The study has stirred up debate among scientists.
tf.why: One leading expert doubts the shapes are blood cells, even though she finds the chemical signs more convincing.

lines.text: Did you hear about the dinosaur bone {{dug up}} in Brazil? Scientists say tiny blood cells {{showed up}} in it.
Blood cells? After 115 million years? So can they {{bring dinosaurs back}} now?
[[The short answer]] is no. The lead scientist {{points out}} that they didn't find any DNA.
Oh. So [[don't get your hopes up]] about a real Jurassic Park.
Right. She even said they haven't found a vial of dinosaur blood.
They {{zoomed in}} with a microscope and saw tiny round shapes. Then chemical tests {{came back}} positive for heme.
It's the part of blood that holds iron. The team says the tests {{back up}} its idea.
But soft parts of the body {{break down}} fast, don't they?
They do. That's why the claim [[raised some eyebrows]]. It has really {{stirred up}} debate.
Does anyone disagree with the team?
Yes. A professor in the U.S. says the shapes look wrong, so they could {{turn out}} to be something else.
[[I see what you mean]]. It's exciting, but it isn't proof yet.
Exactly. The team can't even {{rule out}} microbes.
I'll [[keep an open mind]] until other scientists check it.
Me too. If it's true, they could {{figure out}} a lot about how dinosaurs lived.
